opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and it's something I've thought about a fair amount. In principle you can do it. If you have a good value function, you can derive a policy by doing a one-step lookahead: for every legal move, apply it, evaluate the resulting position with the value network, and pick the move that leads to the best value. That's essentially an implicit policy, like in Q-learning, where acting greedily with respect to your value estimates gives you a policy for free.

The problem is cost and sharpness. In Go you have up to around 361 legal moves, so you'd need hundreds of value network forward passes just to get the prior at a single node, versus one pass for a policy head that spits out a distribution over all moves at once. Inside MCTS, where you're expanding thousands of nodes, that multiplies quickly. So the policy head is really an amortization: it learns to predict, in one shot, what the search would conclude, which is what makes the search tractable.

There's also a quality issue. Value estimates are noisy, and when you take an argmax or softmax over hundreds of noisy estimates, you tend to pick moves whose value happens to be overestimated. It's the same maximization bias you see in Q-learning. The policy head, trained to imitate the visit distribution from search, gives a smoother, better-calibrated prior over which moves deserve exploration. The two heads complement each other: the policy tells you where to look, and the value tells you how good it is once you get there.

That said, I think it's a great experiment to try, especially at small scale, say on a 9x9 board where the branching factor is manageable. You could compare a value-derived prior against a learned policy head and see how much search strength you lose per unit of compute. My guess is the value-derived version is competitive in raw move quality but loses badly on efficiency, and that's ultimately why the AlphaGo design looks the way it does. It's a good lesson for other domains too, including language models: amortizing search into a fast policy is often what makes the whole system practical.

r001.rationale: It proposes choosing the best child by value and mentions softmax over estimates, but does not clearly propose normalizing the child values to produce a policy distribution.

r002.rationale: It says the policy head produces a distribution in one pass, making search tractable, and describes the policy as guiding where to look during MCTS.

r003.rationale: It describes the policy and value heads as complementary, but gives no case where the policy assigns high probability to an action the value head rates poorly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I've thought about a lot, because it gets at something fundamental about why we have policies and value functions as separate objects at all.

In principle, you don't need a policy head. If you have a perfect value function, the policy is implied: just enumerate the legal moves, evaluate the resulting states, and pick the best one. That's the one-step lookahead argument, and it's basically how a lot of classic game engines worked. So in that sense, yes, you could replace the policy head with argmax over value evaluations.

But in practice I think it's a bad trade for AlphaGo specifically, for a few reasons.

The first is compute. Go has a branching factor of a couple hundred. The policy head gives you a prior over all of those moves in a single forward pass. If you want to derive that same distribution from the value function, you need a couple hundred forward passes, one per child state. That's two orders of magnitude more expensive just to get a prior, before you've even started the tree search. And MCTS relies on that prior being cheap, because it's what lets you focus the search on a handful of plausible moves instead of expanding everything.

The second reason is about what the value function actually learns. Value functions trained from self-play are notoriously noisy, especially early in the game, where the outcome is far away and the signal is diluted. The differences between the values of adjacent good moves can be smaller than the noise floor of the network. So if you argmax over those, you're often just amplifying estimation error. The policy head, by contrast, is trained to imitate the result of the full search, which is a much smoother and more informative target. You can think of the policy as a distilled version of search over value, and that distillation is doing real work.

The third thing, and this is the one I find most interesting, is that the policy and the value are learning different things even when they're sharing a trunk. The value head has to answer "who's winning here," which is a global, holistic question. The policy head has to answer "where should I look next," which is more local and more about pattern recognition. Humans do this too. Strong players don't evaluate every move and pick the best; they have an immediate intuition for the three or four candidate moves and then they calculate. Collapsing that into value-only is kind of like asking someone to play by only ever asking "how do I feel about this position" with no intuition for candidate moves.

Now, I don't want to be too dismissive, because there's a real argument on the other side. The nice thing about a value-only approach is that it's more general. The policy head is tied to the action space of the game. If you're in a setting where the action space is huge or continuous, like robotics, a learned value function plus some kind of optimization over actions is often the more practical thing. That's basically what Q-learning methods do. And there's a line of work where you train the value function with an eye toward it being used this way, so it's more calibrated across sibling states rather than just absolutely accurate. If you do that, the gap narrows.

So my overall assessment is: it's possible, it's a legitimate design, and in some domains it's the right one. But for Go, with its discrete, enumerable action space, the policy head is a very efficient compression of search, and throwing it away in favor of value-only lookahead means paying a lot more compute for a worse prior. The really interesting question to me is whether you can get the best of both, where the policy is explicitly derived from the value function through some amortized process, rather than being a separate head trained on a separate target. That feels closer to how I'd want a general agent to work.

r001.rationale: The response proposes choosing the child with the highest value estimate; it does not propose normalizing child values into a policy distribution.

r002.rationale: It says the policy head provides a prior over all moves in one forward pass, letting MCTS focus on plausible moves instead of expanding everything.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe a high-probability policy action receiving a poor rating from the value head.

astra-6.text:
In principle, you can do that. You can evaluate the position after each legal move and choose the move with the highest value—accounting for the fact that it’s then your opponent’s turn. If your value function were perfect, you wouldn’t need a separate policy network.

The practical issue is computation. In Go, you might have hundreds of legal moves. A policy network gives you a distribution over all of them in one forward pass, whereas deriving that distribution from a value network means evaluating all those successor positions. You can batch those evaluations, but you’re still doing substantially more work.

And the value function isn’t perfect. If you maximize over a lot of noisy estimates, you can select a move because its value is overestimated. Search helps check those estimates, and the policy helps focus that search on promising moves. So I think of the policy as amortizing some of the work of figuring out which actions are worth considering. You can replace it with value evaluations, but whether that’s a good trade depends on your compute budget and how reliable your value function is.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing the highest-valued move and evaluating all successor positions, but does not propose normalizing the children’s value estimates into a policy distribution.

r002.rationale: It says the policy network produces a distribution over all legal moves in one forward pass and helps focus search on promising moves, conveying how it narrows search.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify a high-probability policy action that the value head rates poorly as an inconsistency between the heads.

sol-6.1.text:
In principle, you can do that. If you have a sufficiently good value function, you can evaluate the positions resulting from each legal move and choose the best one. The policy is implicit in the value function.

The catch is computational cost. Instead of one forward pass that gives you a distribution over moves, you need to evaluate a bunch of successor states. And if your value estimates have errors, maximizing over them can select a move precisely because you overestimated it.

So the policy head is useful even if it’s theoretically redundant. It gives you a cheap proposal for where to spend your search budget. The value function tells you how promising a position is; the policy helps you avoid having to examine every possibility to find the promising ones. You can derive a policy from value evaluations, but then the question is whether that’s the best use of your inference compute.

r001.rationale: It says to choose the best move from successor-state values, but does not propose normalizing the children’s value estimates into a policy distribution.

r002.rationale: It says the policy head produces a move distribution in one forward pass and helps avoid examining every possibility, communicating its role in narrowing search.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a high-probability policy action that the value head rates poorly or identify such a mismatch as an inconsistency.
